title: John of the Cross, again
tomorrow: a monk said everyone wears a mask. so who's underneath?

lines: A ROPE OF CLOTH, A WINDOW, THE STREET.
cards: Three in the morning is its own country. The phone is face-down, the ceiling feels too close, and every worry has a microphone. A friar in Spain knew that hour better than most.

It's night in Toledo. He's locked in a cramped cell with little light, put there by men of his own religious order who opposed his reforms. And in the dark he's making up poems, holding every line in his memory.
One night, tradition says, he knots strips of cloth into a rope, lowers himself from a window and slips away through the streets. So why would he later write about that kind of night as a gift?

teach.b: He's John of the Cross, and the poem he carried out of that cell begins, in his Spanish, en una noche oscura: on a dark night.
A soul slips out of a quiet house, unseen, with no light to guide it except the one burning in its own heart.
He later wrote whole books unpacking that poem, and the dark night became his name for something that happens in prayer. The sweetness fades.
The old feeling of closeness goes flat. Prayer that used to glow feels like talking to a wall.

teach.h: NOT PROOF THAT GOD HAS GONE.
teach.b: John's surprise is that this isn't proof God has gone. His books say the night loosens our grip on the good feelings, so love can grow for God himself, not just for the glow.
Something to tell a friend tonight: people now say dark night of the soul about any rough season.
John meant something narrower and stranger, a darkness that teaches. Not every hard night is that one.
Grief and depression need people and real help, and if a night ever feels dangerous, call or text 988 in the US, or local emergency help. But looking back down the mountain, John's claim is simple.
He walked out of that cell carrying poems.

how: Catholics honor John of the Cross as a saint and a Doctor of the Church; spiritual directors draw on his books to help people through dryness in prayer.

games.q: what does “john of the cross” mean?
o: a Spanish friar who wrote of the dark night
an English bishop who wrote of the cross
a desert hermit who never wrote a word

games.q: the night and the friar — tap the pairs.
p: where he was locked in a cell
a darkness in prayer that teaches
the one burning in the heart

s: John of the Cross meant any bad week by 'dark night'
he meant a darkness in prayer that teaches; the looser use is how people talk now.
his poem begins 'en una noche oscura'
the lesson says to sit out depression alone, in silence
grief and depression need people and real help; 988 in the US if a night feels dangerous.

games.q: a friend says prayer has felt flat for months and she's sure it means she's doing it wrong. what would John of the Cross say first?
o: flatness isn't proof God has gone; the dark can teach.
she should stop praying until the feeling comes back.
a dark night means her faith is broken somewhere.
games.why: John called that dryness part of the dark night: it loosens our grip on the good feelings so love can grow for God himself.

practice: Find a pen and anything to write on. Remember one night, or one hard stretch, that taught you something you still carry, and write down only what it taught, in a few words.
Rest your hand on the page for the sit; anyone who prays can offer it to God along with the night it came from.

wordCard.voice: John of the Cross. A Spanish friar and poet who named the dark night, a darkness in prayer that teaches.

carryVoice: Your line: the night taught. He walked out of that cell with a poem. See you tomorrow.
